posts.title: Yaru theme style guide
posts.html:
This post collects the visual elements of the Yaru theme and the options you can change in the Ghost admin. Use it as a reference when writing: everything here comes out of Ghost's standard editor, with no special HTML.

Palette

The theme follows Ubuntu 24.04's Yaru dark: charcoal surfaces, light text and the Ubuntu orange only in the details (cursor, active tab, links, buttons and focus).

Background
#1d1d1d
Surface
#242424
Headerbar
#303030
Terminal
#171421
Headings
#f6f6f6
Body
#c4c4c4
Secondary
#8f8f8f
Ubuntu orange
#e95420
Prompt: user
#8ae234
Prompt: path
#729fcf

The orange comes from Ghost's Accent color (Design & branding → Brand). Recommended: #E95420.

Typography

Text is set in Ubuntu Sans; code, metadata and prompts in Ubuntu Sans Mono. Both fonts ship with the theme. If you pick another font in Design & branding → Typography, it replaces Ubuntu Sans.

A paragraph with bold, italic, a link and inline code. Body text uses a softer grey than headings, so long reads are easier on the eyes on a dark background.

Heading level 2

Use H2 for the main sections of a post.

Heading level 3

Use H3 for subsections.

Heading level 4

Use H4 for smaller groups.

Lists

  • Unordered list item
  • Second item with bold
  • Third item
  1. First step
  2. Second step
    1. Sub-step
  3. Third step

Quotes

Default quote: italic, light text and an accent-colored bar on the left.
Alternative quote: larger and without the bar. In the editor, click the quote button twice.

Code

With code_blocks_as_windows on, every code block becomes a GNOME window. The window title is the language picked in the editor's code card.

With syntax_highlighting on, code gets the Ubuntu terminal colors: keywords, strings, numbers, functions, tags and properties, variables, and comments in grey. It works with JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, HTML, CSS, SCSS, Handlebars, JSON, YAML, Markdown, Bash, Dockerfile, Nginx, INI, TOML, diff, SQL, GraphQL, Python, Ruby, ERB, PHP, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, C, C++, C#, Swift, Lua and Elixir.

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.interface color-scheme 'prefer-dark'
// Greeting with a template string
const greet = (name, times = 1) => {
  if (!name) return null;
  return `Hello, ${name}!`.repeat(times);
};
class Post < ApplicationRecord
  # Posts published in the last 30 days
  scope :recent, -> { where(published_at: 30.days.ago..) }

  def short_title(limit = 40)
    title.truncate(limit)
  end
end
.gh-content pre {
  color: #e6e6e6;
  background-color: var(--color-terminal-bg);
  border-radius: 12px;
}

To change how code blocks look, use the code_style option: Yaru or Ray.so.

Without a language, the window is titled "Terminal":

$ uname -a
Linux yaru 6.8.0-generic x86_64 GNU/Linux

Images

Cards

💡
Accent callout, for tips and important notes.
📌
Grey callout, for neutral remarks.
Accent button

Frequently asked question (toggle)

The answer stays hidden until the reader clicks.
ElementFontColor
HeadingsUbuntu Sans#f6f6f6
BodyUbuntu Sans#c4c4c4
MetadataUbuntu Sans Mono#8f8f8f

Theme options

All of them live in Settings → Design & branding → Customize, split across the panel's tabs.

Site-wide

  • terminal_prompt — user@host of the terminal prompt (home, breadcrumb, tag, author, 404). Empty = just ~$. Default: guest@localhost.
  • projects_tag — Slug of the portfolio tag. Its posts are left out of /blog/ and it doesn't show up in the category pills. Default: projects.
  • prompt_search — Title search in the prompt on the home, tag and author pages: type after the $ and the list is filtered. / focuses the search, Enter opens the first result and Esc clears it. Default: on.
  • show_blinking_cursor — Blinking orange cursor in the search prompt. Default: on.
  • signup_heading — Heading of the newsletter block (end of posts and footer). Default: site title.
  • signup_subheading — Text of the newsletter block. Default: site description.
  • github_url — Link to your GitHub profile. The icon shows up in the footer, after the social accounts set in Ghost. Default: empty.

Homepage

  • show_home_intro — Large intro sentence at the top of the home page. Default: on.
  • home_intro_text — The intro sentence (only shown with the option above on). Default: site description.
  • show_post_numbers — 01, 02… numbering in the post list. Default: on.
  • show_author — "BY AUTHOR" in the list metadata. Default: on.
  • show_reading_time — Reading time in the list. Default: on.
  • show_publish_date — Publish date in the list. Default: off.

Post

  • show_breadcrumb — Prompt-style breadcrumb (~/tag$) at the top of posts and pages. Default: on.
  • code_blocks_as_windows — Code blocks as GNOME windows, like the ones in the Code section. Default: on.
  • code_style — Colors inside the code window: Yaru (Ubuntu terminal colors) or Ray.so (the same GNOME window, with a purple background, semibold text and pink, yellow, green and cyan colors). Default: Yaru.
  • syntax_highlighting — Syntax colors in code blocks. Default: on.
  • show_post_signup — Newsletter block at the end of posts. Default: on.
  • show_related_articles — "Read next": three numbered posts that share tags with the current one. Default: on.

Recommended Ghost setup

  • Accent color: #E95420.
  • Primary navigation: a few short items, such as Home, Blog, Projects and About. Categories live in the pills on the Blog and tag pages. The current page gets the orange bar; items that don't fit go into the ⋮ menu.
  • Secondary navigation: footer links (e.g. About, RSS, Subscribe → #/portal/signup).
  • Social accounts (Settings → General): filled-in accounts show up as icons in the footer. GitHub comes from the theme's github_url option.
  • Logo: optional. Without one, the title is set in mono, exactly as written in Ghost.
  • Language: Settings → General → Publication language. The theme ships with English and Brazilian Portuguese.
  • Tags: the primary tag shows up in the metadata and the breadcrumb; "Read next" uses shared tags.
  • Members: with members enabled, Sign in/Subscribe show up in the header along with the newsletter block.

posts.html:
Turbo 8 added page refreshes with morphing: instead of replacing the whole page, Turbo compares the new HTML with the current one and only changes what's different. Scroll position, focus and form state survive.

Turn it on

<%# app/views/layouts/application.html.erb %>
<%= turbo_refreshes_with method: :morph, scroll: :preserve %>

Broadcast a refresh

Instead of crafting a Turbo Stream for every change, tell everyone looking at a record to refresh. Morphing makes it cheap.

class Board < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :cards
  broadcasts_refreshes
end

class Card < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :board, touch: true
end
<%= turbo_stream_from @board %>

Gotchas

  • Elements with state you want to keep, like an open dropdown, need data-turbo-permanent.
  • Stimulus controllers reconnect on morph: keep connect() idempotent.
  • Broadcast refreshes are debounced, so a burst of changes becomes one refresh.

posts.html:
Kamal deploys Docker containers to any server you can SSH into. Version 2 ships with kamal-proxy, which handles zero-downtime deploys and automatic HTTPS, so a VPS and a domain are all you need.

The whole config

# config/deploy.yml
service: shop
image: acme/shop

servers:
  web:
    - 203.0.113.10
  job:
    hosts:
      - 203.0.113.10
    cmd: bin/jobs

proxy:
  ssl: true
  host: shop.example.com

registry:
  username: acme
  password:
    - KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD

env:
  secret:
    - RAILS_MASTER_KEY

Deploying

kamal setup     # first time: installs Docker, boots the proxy and the app
kamal deploy    # every time after that
kamal app logs -f
kamal rollback <version>

Secrets

Secrets go in .kamal/secrets, which can read them from a password manager instead of storing them in plain text:

KAMAL_REGISTRY_PASSWORD=$(op read "op://Deploy/registry/password")
RAILS_MASTER_KEY=$(cat config/master.key)

Do I need Kubernetes?

Probably not. A couple of well-sized servers behind Kamal handle a lot of traffic, and you can read the entire deployment setup in one file.

posts.title: Context engineering for coding agents
posts.html:
Prompt engineering was about finding the magic words. Context engineering is about deciding what the model sees: which rules, which files, which tools, and when. For coding agents it matters more than the model you pick.

The layers

LayerLoadedExample
RulesAlways"Commit messages in English"
SkillsOn demand"How we write service objects"
ToolsWhen calledIssue tracker, staging database, browser
HooksOn eventsRun the linter after every edit

Keep the rules file short

Everything in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md is read on every turn. Long files dilute the instructions that matter. Keep it to conventions that apply everywhere and point to skills for the rest.

# Project rules

- Ruby 3.4, Rails 8. Run `bin/rails test` before saying you're done.
- Business logic goes in `app/services`, one public `call` method.
- Never edit files in `db/schema.rb` by hand; write a migration.
- For anything about specs, load the `rspec` skill.

Skills: knowledge on demand

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md. Its description is what the agent reads to decide whether to load it, so it has to say when to use it and when not to.

---
name: rails-services
description: Conventions for service objects. Use whenever you implement business
  logic that writes data, calls external APIs or spans a transaction.
  Don't use it for simple reads (see rails-queries).
---

# Service objects
1. One public method: `call`.
2. Return a result object; never raise for control flow.
3. Wrap database writes in a transaction, never HTTP calls.

Hooks: automatic feedback

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "bin/agent-lint" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}
💡
Start with the skills that fix the mistakes you keep pointing out in code review. They pay for themselves in the first week.

posts.html:
The Model Context Protocol lets AI assistants call tools you define. If your product runs on Rails, a small MCP endpoint lets an assistant search orders, read a customer's history or open a support ticket, with the same authorization rules as the rest of your app.

Install the SDK

bundle add mcp

Define a tool

A tool is a class with a description, an input schema and a call method. The description is what the model reads to decide when to use it, so be specific.

class SearchOrdersTool < MCP::Tool
  tool_name "search_orders"
  description "Search the current user's orders by status or product name"

  input_schema(
    properties: {
      query: { type: "string" },
      status: { type: "string", enum: %w[pending paid shipped cancelled] }
    },
    required: ["query"]
  )

  annotations(read_only_hint: true)

  def self.call(query:, server_context:, status: nil)
    orders = server_context[:user].orders.search(query)
    orders = orders.where(status:) if status

    MCP::Tool::Response.new([{ type: "text", text: orders.limit(20).to_json(only: %i[id status total]) }])
  end
end

Expose it from a controller

class McpController < ActionController::API
  include Authentication # your token-based auth

  def create
    server = MCP::Server.new(
      name: "shop",
      tools: [SearchOrdersTool],
      server_context: { user: Current.user }
    )

    render json: server.handle_json(request.body.read)
  end
end

Guardrails

  • Scope everything to the user. Pass the authenticated user through server_context, never trust IDs from the model.
  • Start read-only. Mark tools with read_only_hint and add writes later, one at a time.
  • Return less. Every byte you return goes into the model's context window.

posts.html:
For years, a new Rails app meant PostgreSQL and Redis: one for data, the other for jobs, cache and Action Cable. Rails 8 ships with the Solid trio, which runs all three on top of the database you already have.

NeedBeforeRails 8 default
Background jobsSidekiq + RedisSolid Queue
CacheRedis / MemcachedSolid Cache
WebSocketsRedis pub/subSolid Cable

Solid Queue

Jobs are rows in a table, picked up with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Recurring jobs live in a YAML file, no extra scheduler needed:

# config/recurring.yml
production:
  clear_abandoned_carts:
    class: ClearAbandonedCartsJob
    schedule: every day at 3am
  sync_exchange_rates:
    command: "ExchangeRate.sync!"
    schedule: every hour

Solid Cache

The cache lives on disk instead of RAM. Disk is cheap, so you can keep a much bigger cache for much longer.

# config/environments/production.rb
config.cache_store = :solid_cache_store

When you still want Redis

  • Very high job throughput, where the extra database load matters.
  • Features that rely on Redis data structures: rate limiting with sorted sets, leaderboards.
  • An existing Sidekiq setup that works. There's no prize for migrating.
🧰
One less service means one less thing to provision, monitor and upgrade. For most apps, that's the real win.

Stack: Go, GitHub API
License: MIT
Status: Active
Repository: github.com/example/skillshelf

A CLI to share AI agent skills across a team: install them from a Git repository, keep them up to date and see who changed what. Example project for the theme.

$ skillshelf add github.com/acme/agent-skills
✔ 14 skills installed in ~/.claude/skills

$ skillshelf outdated
rails-services   1.2.0 → 1.3.0   "Add transaction rules"
rspec            0.9.1 → 1.0.0   "Spec tree before code"

$ skillshelf update

Why

Skills copied by hand drift apart within a week. With a shelf, changing a skill is a pull request, and everyone gets the new version with one command.

Configuration

# .skillshelf.yml
sources:
  - repo: github.com/acme/agent-skills
    ref: main
target: ~/.claude/skills
pin:
  rspec: 0.9.1

posts.html:
Asking a coding agent to "build this feature" works until the feature touches more than a handful of files. After that, the agent guesses what you meant, and guessing is expensive. Spec-Driven Development flips the order: write the spec first, then the code, with a human approval between every step.

The flow

  1. PRD: the problem, who it affects and numbered acceptance criteria (AC01, AC02…).
  2. Tech spec: alternatives with trade-offs, the recommendation, the design and a matrix linking every acceptance criterion to a test.
  3. Tasks: small, sequential deliverables, each with its own tests.
  4. Implementation: one task at a time, followed by an automated review against the project's conventions.
🧭
The golden rule: the agent never moves to the next phase on its own. Every phase ends with “approved?” and only continues on a yes.

Everything is a file

Each phase produces a file that lives next to the code. The nice side effect: the pull request arrives with the why already written down.

docs/specs/pix-checkout/
├── prd.md           # problem, scope and acceptance criteria
├── techspec.md      # alternatives, decision and design
├── tasks.md         # overview and progress
├── 1_task.md        # one small deliverable, with tests
├── 1_review.md      # automated review against the conventions
└── .flow.yml        # flow state, so you can resume later
feature: pix-checkout
phase: implement
branch: feat/pix-checkout
tasks:
  - { n: 1, title: "Create the Pix charge at checkout", status: done }
  - { n: 2, title: "Confirm payment through the webhook", status: in_progress }
  - { n: 3, title: "Show the payment status on the order", status: pending }

What changes day to day

  • Less rework: product questions show up in the PRD, not in code review.
  • Smaller PRs: every task becomes a reviewable commit.
  • Context that survives: you can pause and come back days later, because the state lives in a file.
The agent writes code faster than I do. The spec makes sure it writes the right code.

Everything is a file

Each phase produces a file that lives next to the code. The nice side effect: the pull request arrives with the why already written down.

docs/specs/pix-checkout/
├── prd.md           # problem, scope and acceptance criteria
├── techspec.md      # alternatives, decision and design
├── tasks.md         # overview and progress
├── 1_task.md        # one small deliverable, with tests
├── 1_review.md      # automated review against the conventions
└── .flow.yml        # flow state, so you can resume later

feature: pix-checkout
phase: implement
branch: feat/pix-checkout
tasks:
  - { n: 1, title: "Create the Pix charge at checkout", status: done }
  - { n: 2, title: "Confirm payment through the webhook", status: in_progress }
  - { n: 3, title: "Show the payment status on the order", status: pending }


What changes day to day

 * Less rework: product questions show up in the PRD, not in code review.
 * Smaller PRs: every task becomes a reviewable commit.
 * Context that survives: you can pause and come back days later, because the state lives in a file.

The agent writes code faster than I do. The spec makes sure it writes the right code.
